headline: Mamba, Diffusion & World Models are candidates to replace LLMs
summary: The dominant AI architecture shifts every few years, and research labs are already developing the next generation of models to overcome current LLM limitations.
details: AI's dominant architecture typically shifts every three years, and the next wave is already emerging in research labs. This article explores the leading candidates poised to replace the transformer model, addressing its inherent limitations.

Transformers, while powerful, face four major challenges: O(n²) self-attention complexity, diminishing returns from scraped internet data, escalating compute costs, and their fundamental limitation as token predictors rather than reasoners.

State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba offer a new approach with linear O(n) scaling. They maintain a compressed internal state, summarizing history efficiently, which allows for constant memory per token during inference regardless of sequence length.

Mamba achieves this efficiency through selective recurrence, dynamically choosing what information to keep in its state. This is implemented via a hardware-aware parallel scan, similar to FlashAttention's optimization for transformers.

Yann LeCun has advocated for "world models, not word predictors," with his team developing Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for images, video, and language. This research points towards models that understand causal relationships in the physical world.

The goal is to provide engineers with practical insights for architecting systems for 2027 and beyond, based on current evidence. The shift is already underway in research, not yet in public announcements.

headline_marked: [[Gen AI Tools Used to Push ‘Slop Jihad’]], radicalizing youth with SpongeBob cartoons
headline: Gen AI Tools Used to Push ‘Slop Jihad’, radicalizing youth with SpongeBob cartoons
summary: A new report reveals how terror groups leverage generative AI to create "Slop Jihad" content, like SpongeBob SquarePants cartoons, making extremist propaganda more accessible to younger audiences on platforms like TikTok.
details: Over a decade ago, the Islamic State released a disturbing video depicting men drowning in a cage. Today, this video has been reproduced as a SpongeBob SquarePants cartoon, showing fish in orange jumpsuits in a cage, lowered by SpongeBob while Squidward films.

This content, shared on TikTok, is part of "Slop Jihad," a trend identified by the Institute of Strategic Dialogue (ISD). Young supporters of groups like ISIS and al-Qaida use generative AI to create fan edits, cartoons, and memes for radicalization.

The ISD report, shared with WIRED, concludes this shift "signals a fundamental transformation in the aesthetics of jihadist propaganda online." Tech Against Terrorism highlights concerns about the growing volume and diversity of material.

Highly stylized AI-generated content can make violent Islamist extremist material more accessible to younger audiences, reducing the visibility of conventional terrorist branding. Users may encounter perpetrator glorification inadvertently, driving algorithmic recommendations to more overt propaganda.

Islamic terror groups have a history of adapting to new media, leveraging emerging technologies for recruitment and decentralized propaganda. This includes the "Alt Jihad" movement and the use of AI-generated anchors by ISIS-affiliated news programs since 2024.

The current look and feel of AI-produced content is markedly different, with Moustafa Ayad of ISD stating it's "new and it's still growing, it has not peaked by any means." It now includes content like SpongeBob SquarePants as the Islamic State.
Generative AI tools are also used to quickly and cheaply turn official terror group content, such as ISIS's weekly al-Naba newsletter, into animated videos like anime for platforms like TikTok.

While some traditional supporters show animosity towards the new aesthetic, many accounts that share official propaganda are also sharing the newer "Slop Jihad" videos, indicating a complex "love-hate relationship."

TikTok has been central to these online messaging campaigns, with its powerful algorithmic recommendations spreading messages. An OECD report in 2024 listed TikTok among the top 10 platforms for terrorist and extremist content.

ISD found 150 "Slop Jihad" videos from 71 accounts on TikTok, accumulating over 5.4 million views. The prevalence is attributed to TikTok's "For You Page" algorithm and an existing jihadist support ecosystem. TikTok has contested the report's findings.
